title: The widow's jar (1 Kings 17:8–16)
hook: a widow shares her last flour, and the jar never runs out

segments.voice: Yesterday, birds brought Elijah his food by the brook. Your line was the ravens fed him. Did help come from somewhere you didn't expect? Today the brook is dry, and the help comes from someone with almost nothing. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

At the gate of a town called Zarephath, a woman is gathering sticks. Not many. Just enough for one small fire. A stranger, dusty from the road, calls out to her: bring me a little water in a vessel, so I can drink. She turns to go and get it. Then he calls after her again: and bring me, please, a piece of bread. She stops. Her answer is blunt, and it tells you everything about her kitchen. Today's word is in that kitchen.
screen: `THE GATE OF ZAREPHATH.` → `A LITTLE WATER, PLEASE.` → `AND A PIECE OF BREAD.`

segments.voice: First Kings seventeen. Zarephath belongs to Zidon, outside the land of Israel. She answers Elijah with an oath, as the LORD your God lives, and then the plain truth: she has nothing baked, only a handful of meal in a jar and a little oil in a cruse. She's gathering a couple of sticks, she says, to make one last meal for herself and her son, so that they can eat it and die. The Hebrew word for her jar is kad. Elijah says: don't be afraid. Go and do as you said, but make me a little cake first, and after that make some for yourself and your son. Because, he says, the LORD has said the jar of meal won't be used up and the cruse of oil won't fail until the day the LORD sends rain. Hear what he's asking. Her last flour. To a stranger. Before her own child. And she does it. The text says she, and he, and her house ate for many days, and in the 1917 Jewish translation: "The jar of meal was not spent, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD." Each day, she reaches into a jar that should be empty, and there's enough for that day. Not a mountain of flour. Enough. Notice who this miracle runs through. Not a king, not a priest. A widow in a town of Zidon, at the end of her supplies, who shares first. And notice how it follows yesterday. Ravens fed Elijah. Now a woman with nothing to spare feeds him. Giving, in this story, doesn't start with plenty. It starts with a handful.
screen: `A WIDOW IN ZAREPHATH OF ZIDON.` · `A HANDFUL OF MEAL, A LITTLE OIL.` · `MAKE ME A CAKE FIRST.` · `ENOUGH, EACH DAY, UNTIL THE RAIN.` · then, large: `NEITHER DID THE CRUSE OF OIL FAIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share from what little you have. Settle, and breathe. Name what feels scarce for you right now: time, money, energy, patience. Don't pretend it's plenty. Just name it honestly, the way the widow did at the gate. Now think of one small thing you could still share from it: ten minutes, a meal, a kind message, a few dollars. Not from the surplus. From the handful. Hold that thought and let it settle. If you pray, you can ask for some of her courage. The bell holds the time.
Kad. The Hebrew word for jar, the one with a widow's last flour that never ran dry. Today's word.
Your line: the jar didn't fail. Today, share one small thing from what feels scarce, and see what's still there tomorrow. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of the widow of Zarephath in the book of Kings, where it is followed in the same chapter by Elijah's prayer for her son.

original.note: Hebrew: a jar. the kad of meal was not used up until the rain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic jar that's always full.
what it means: a widow in Zidon's land gives her last flour to a stranger, and there is enough each day until the rain.
what a scholar hears: kad, her jar, is the same Hebrew word as the pitcher Rebekah carries to the well in Genesis 24.

sources.quoted: The jar of meal was not spent, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD

notes: 'Belongs to Zidon' paraphrases 17:9; 'isn't an Israelite' is an inference from the location, widely held; confirm wording.
'Many days' (17:15) is paraphrased without a number.

Editor: the text never says the widow is not an Israelite, so the teach, screen, myth and trapdoor now say only what 17:9–12 says (Zarephath belongs to Zidon; she swears by the LORD your God, Elijah's God); removed a 'think about' formula.
